author: high
claim: Subgoal 1 solved: count maximal chains and those containing a fixed k-element set.
evidence: A maximal chain has exactly one set of each size 0,...,n and is uniquely obtained by ordering the n ground elements and adjoining them successively, so there are n! maximal chains. For a fixed k-set A, a corresponding ordering yields a chain containing A exactly when its first k positions contain exactly A. The first k positions may be ordered in k! ways and the remaining positions in (n-k)! ways. Thus A belongs to k!(n-k)! maximal chains.

links.subgoal: Count maximal chains and incidences with a fixed k-set.

glossary.n: the size of the ground set [n]

author: high
claim: Subgoal 2 solved: derive the LYM inequality for the antichain.
evidence: Double-count pairs (A,C), where A is in the antichain and C is a maximal chain containing A. A chain cannot contain two distinct antichain members because every two sets in one chain are comparable. Hence there are at most n! pairs. By the fixed-set count, the number is sum over A of |A|!(n-|A|)!. Dividing by n! gives sum over A of 1/binom(n,|A|)<=1.

links.subgoal: Use the antichain condition to derive the LYM inequality.

glossary.C: a maximal chain of subsets of [n]
glossary.n: the size of the ground set [n]

author: high
claim: Subgoal 3 solved: convert the LYM inequality to the Sperner bound and verify sharpness.
evidence: The ratio binom(n,k+1)/binom(n,k)=(n-k)/(k+1) shows the binomial coefficients increase to the middle and decrease afterward, so M=binom(n,floor(n/2)) is maximal. Therefore each LYM summand 1/binom(n,|A|) is at least 1/M, giving |family|/M<=1. The family of all floor(n/2)-subsets has M members, and no two distinct equal-size sets contain one another, so it is an antichain attaining equality.

links.subgoal: Use maximality of the middle binomial coefficient to derive the bound and verify the middle-level construction.
links.attempt_summary: Solved by the adjacent-ratio proof of binomial unimodality and a same-size incomparability check.
